summary: Adversarially audit the ferro embedded-Python apps demo: memory claims, "apps actually run" honesty, integration correctness, and doc accuracy. Read-only; verify each finding before reporting.

confirmed.title: The "64 MB ceiling" is thread-count-dependent, not a true ceiling: it breaks at 8 threads (78 MB)
confirmed.claim: 00-DEMO.md L21/L32 frames "Eager (worst case)" / "the pathological eager ceiling" as a worst case, tested only up to 4 threads.
confirmed.evidence: Running the same eager write-storm at `--threads 8` peaks at 78.4 MB RSS (PSS 72.3 / USS 70.6), "under 64 MB: NO". The per-thread cost (2MB stack + SQLite page cache + per-request allocations) scales linearly, so 4 threads is not a ceiling — it is the largest thread count that happens to (barely) fit. The report calls 4T the "worst case" and "the pathological eager ceiling" without stating the result is specific to a thread count.
confirmed.fix: Either cap/justify the deployment at 4 threads explicitly (and state that >4 threads in eager mode exceeds 64 MB), or relabel the 4T number as "4-thread peak" rather than "the ceiling / worst case". The lazy config should be the recommended one since it has headroom for more threads.
confirmed.reasoning: The finding is substantiated both empirically and textually. EMPIRICAL: Re-running the exact recommended config (run-ferrod.sh / bench.sh allocator + 256KB cache) on the prebuilt binary at higher thread counts reproduces the finding's numbers: eager 4T peaks RSS ~64.1-64.7 MB (matches report), eager 6T ~71.3 MB, eager 8T ~77-78.2 MB with PSS up to 72.1 and USS up to 70.4 — every metric well over 64 MB (the report's own "under 64 MB" test = NO). This matches the finding's cited 78.4/72.3/70.6 closely and confirms roughly linear ~3.5 MB/thread scaling, i.e. 4 threads is the largest count that (barely) fits, not a true ceiling. TEXTUAL: The report repeatedly labels the 4-thread eager number as "pathological worst case" (00-DEMO.md L22, L33), "the ceiling" (L32), and titles its levers section "to get the eager ceiling under 64 MB" (L144); run-ferrod.sh L13 calls its config "the configuration under which the all-apps-eager worst case stays within 64 MB." "Ceiling"/"worst case" denote an upper bound, but the eager number is not bounded — it grows past 64 MB by the very next thread step. The report nowhere states that >4 eager threads exceeds 64 MB, nor does it cap the deployment at 4 threads; the bench script only sweeps T=1,2,4. So a non-bounding, thread-count-specific figure is presented as the bounding worst case — a genuine overstatement. PARTIAL MITIGATION (why not higher than high): the report IS transparent that 64.1 is a 4-thread measurement (it is in the table cell and prose), and it already flags 4T eager RSS as "just over" 64, and it recommends lazy mode (which I confirmed survives 8T at 54.4 MB). But disclosing the measured number's thread count does not cure mislabeling it "the ceiling / worst case," and the breakage at 8T is real and undisclosed. The finding's suggested fix (relabel as "4-thread peak" and state >4 eager threads exceeds 64 MB, or cap eager at 4 threads, recommending lazy which has headroom) is correct and supported by the data (lazy 8T=54.4 MB, lazy only breaks at ~16T=79.9 MB).

confirmed.title: Write-storm workload reads 10 of 12 tables that are completely empty, understating the memory peak
confirmed.claim: 00-DEMO.md L123/L29: "Peak under a concurrent write-storm (12 reads + 2 writes per round)" presented as a representative/realistic load proving 64 MB holds.
confirmed.evidence: ferrod.rs:628-631 reads from 12 doctypes per round, but in the demo site (/home/frappe/ferro-demo/site/db/_d3b3bc5c1c1a19aa.db) only 2 of those tables have any rows: tabCRM Deal=1476 and tabToDo=1472; the other 10 (CRM Lead, HD Ticket, GP Project, Employee, Sales Invoice, Item, Customer, Contact, Sales Order, Purchase Invoice) are all 0 rows. The two non-empty reads use limit_page_length=5, so each read materializes at most 5 rows. The reads exercise routing/meta/SQL but touch almost no row data, so the per-request working set (and thus the sampled peak) is artificially small relative to a real workload returning real result sets.
confirmed.fix: Populate the read doctypes with representative row counts (e.g., thousands of Employee/Item/Sales Invoice rows) and read realistic page sizes (e.g., 20-100 rows with multiple fields), then re-measure. A peak measured against mostly-empty tables is not evidence the 64 MB budget holds under real read load.
confirmed.reasoning:
The finding is substantiated and, if anything, understated. Verified directly:

CODE: /home/frappe/ferro/src/ferrod.rs:628-631 lists the 12 read doctypes; line 675 builds the URL `/api/resource/{}?limit_page_length=5` with NO `fields` param. build_list_query (ferrod.rs:405-432) only sets q.fields when a `fields` param is present, so the default ListQuery applies. ListQuery::default() (orm.rs:119-130) sets `fields: vec!["name"]`. get_list (orm.rs:300-323) therefore selects ONLY the `name` column. So every list read in the write-storm returns at most 5 rows of a single short column — never the 25-57 columns of real row data.

DATA: Querying /home/frappe/ferro-demo/site/db/_d3b3bc5c1c1a19aa.db, 9 of 12 read tables are empty (CRM Lead, HD Ticket, GP Project, Employee, Sales Invoice, Item, Customer, Sales Order, Purchase Invoice = 0 rows). Only CRM Deal (3479) and ToDo (3569) are populated (Contact=5). Emulating the exact read SQL per round: total result payload ≈195 bytes (CRM Deal 95B, ToDo 50B, Contact 50B); the other 9 reads return 0 rows / 0 bytes.

RUN: `ferrod loadtest ... --load lazy --threads 4 --rounds 8` -> 448 requests, 0 errors, peak RSS 39.2 MB (matches report's 39.3). Reads against the empty tables all succeed, confirming they materialize nothing.

SCOPE: This hardcoded loadtest is the ONLY benchmark feeding the entire RESULTS.txt memory matrix; there is no realistic/read-heavy/wide-field benchmark anywhere (even verify.sh reads use fields=["name"]). The report frames these write-storm peaks (00-DEMO.md L20-37, L128-141) as proof that the 64 MB budget holds for "the realistic deployment." A read mix whose entire materialized result set is ~195 bytes/round (mostly empty tables, name-only, <=5 rows) is not representative of real Frappe list-view load (dozens of rows x many fields + link title fetches), so the sampled read-side working set, and thus the peak, understates a real workload.

Minor inaccuracies in the finding that do NOT change the conclusion: the cited absolute row counts are stale (the loadtest appends CRM Deal/ToDo rows each run, so they've grown; Contact is now 5, not 0). The structural point — 9-10 of 12 reads empty, name-only, <=5 rows — is fully confirmed and the finding actually misses the strongest detail (single-column `name`-only select).

confirmed.title: Recorded idle PSS/USS run ~1 MB below what the current binary reproduces (consistently optimistic, never pessimistic)
confirmed.claim: RESULTS.txt L15-16 / 00-DEMO.md L119-120: erpnext eager idle PSS=35.8/USS=33.8; all-5 eager idle PSS=43.5/USS=41.6.
confirmed.evidence: Re-running `ferrod measure` with the recommended config: erpnext eager idle reproduces RSS=42.7 (matches) but PSS=36.7/USS=35.0 (recorded 35.8/33.8 — ~1 MB higher than recorded). All-5 eager idle reproduces RSS=50.5 (matches) but PSS=44.5/USS=42.8 (recorded 43.5/41.6 — again ~1 MB higher). RSS matches exactly every time; the shareable-memory columns recorded in the matrix are ~1 MB lower than current reality, and the direction is always optimistic. Minor (within PSS noise from concurrent libpython mappers), but worth re-snapshotting since the report leans on PSS/USS for the "under 64" framing of the borderline case.
confirmed.fix: Regenerate RESULTS.txt against the current binary and average over a few runs, or note the ~1 MB run-to-run variance on PSS/USS so the recorded single-sample values aren't read as exact.
confirmed.reasoning:
The finding claims RESULTS.txt L15-16 / 00-DEMO.md L119-125 record idle PSS/USS values ~1 MB lower (more optimistic) than the current binary reproduces, while RSS matches exactly, and that the bias is always optimistic. I reproduced this exactly with the recommended config (run-ferrod.sh).

erpnext eager idle: recorded PSS=35.8/USS=33.8. Four reruns gave PSS=36.6-36.7, USS=34.9-35.0 — about +0.8-0.9 MB PSS and +1.1-1.2 MB USS over recorded. RSS reproduced 42.6-42.7, matching recorded 42.7.

all-5 eager idle: recorded PSS=43.5/USS=41.6. Reproduced PSS=44.4-44.5, USS=42.7-42.8 — about +0.9-1.1 MB over recorded. RSS reproduced 50.4-50.5, matching recorded 50.5. (Loadtest post-boot idle also showed PSS=44.5/USS=42.8, corroborating.)

The offset is consistent in sign (recorded is always lower / more favorable) and has tiny run-to-run variance (±0.1 MB across runs), so this is a real systematic ~1 MB optimistic skew on the shareable-memory columns, not random noise. RSS — the column the report uses for the headline 64 MB framing — matches the matrix exactly every time.

Minor inaccuracies in the finding text: it cites the reproduced erpnext as PSS=36.7/USS=35.0 (I measured 36.6-36.7/34.9-35.0) and all-5 as PSS=44.5/USS=42.8 (I measured 44.4-44.5/42.7-42.8); these are within my observed range and do not change the substance. Severity 'low' is appropriate: the idle case is far from the 64 MB line so the optimism doesn't flip any under/over verdict for these rows. The finding correctly characterizes the issue and its suggested fix (re-snapshot / note variance) is reasonable.

confirmed.title: Demo cites CRMSalesHierarchy.validate as proven-real controller execution, but it is silently dropped and never runs
confirmed.claim: 00-DEMO.md line 181: "the app controller's own lifecycle methods execute as real Python (proven: RetentionBonus.validate, CRMSalesHierarchy.validate, CRMDeal create)."
confirmed.evidence: crm/crm/fcrm/doctype/crm_sales_hierarchy/crm_sales_hierarchy.py declares `class CRMSalesHierarchy(NestedSet)` importing `from frappe.utils.nestedset import NestedSet`. That module is not in the shim; ferro_boot's _LazyFinder (shim/ferro_boot.py:36-53) resolves it, and `NestedSet` becomes `frappe._lazy.Stub` (verified: `ns.NestedSet is Stub == True`). `_register_module_controllers` (ferro_boot.py:128-135) requires `issubclass(obj, _Document)`, which fails, so the class is NEVER registered. Introspection: `'CRM Sales Hierarchy' in frappe._CONTROLLER_REGISTRY == False` and it is not even in needs_python_registry(). End-to-end via the real binary: POSTing two `CRM Sales Hierarchy` rows with the same `user` both return HTTP 200 (names 4528ceda14 and d64561bd73), whereas the real validate throws "User {0} is already mapped to hierarchy node {1}." verify.sh contains zero references to Sales Hierarchy, so this claimed proof is never actually exercised.
confirmed.fix: Remove CRMSalesHierarchy.validate from the list of proven-executing controllers, OR port frappe.utils.nestedset (and the other framework base classes) so NestedSet-based controllers actually register and run. At minimum, verify.sh must test a controller whose base is a framework class, not only RetentionBonus(Document).
confirmed.reasoning:
The finding is fully substantiated and I could not refute it. 00-DEMO.md line 183 explicitly lists `CRMSalesHierarchy.validate` among controllers "proven" to execute as real Python, but the controller is silently dropped and its validate never runs.

Mechanism (verified at every step):
- /home/frappe/ferro-apps-investigation/repos/crm/crm/fcrm/doctype/crm_sales_hierarchy/crm_sales_hierarchy.py declares `class CRMSalesHierarchy(NestedSet)` and imports `from frappe.utils.nestedset import NestedSet`. Its real validate calls frappe.throw("User {0} is already mapped to hierarchy node {1}.") on a duplicate user.
- The shim has no frappe/utils/nestedset module (shim/frappe/utils/ contains only __init__.py and data.py). So ferro_boot's _LazyFinder (shim/ferro_boot.py:36-53, appended last to sys.meta_path) resolves frappe.utils.nestedset to a lazy stub module, and NestedSet becomes frappe._lazy.Stub.
- Stub is `class Stub(metaclass=_Meta): pass` — it subclasses object, not Document. So `class CRMSalesHierarchy(NestedSet)` becomes `class CRMSalesHierarchy(Stub)`.
- _register_module_controllers (ferro_boot.py:128-135) gates registration on `issubclass(obj, _Document)`, which is False, so the class is never registered and the function returns None.

The two OTHER proofs in the same sentence (RetentionBonus.validate, CRMDeal create) are genuine — RetentionBonus(Document) and CRMDeal(Document) subclass Document directly, register fine, and verify.sh steps 2-4 exercise them and pass. Only the CRMSalesHierarchy.validate claim is the overstatement. Severity "critical" is somewhat aggressive given the broader "the apps run" claim is partly true and the honesty section itself acknowledges framework-internal reach-throughs no-op; but the specific named "proven" claim is concretely false and never tested, which is a real, file-level overstatement.

confirmed.title: 20 core master doctypes silently lose ALL controller logic; demo mischaracterizes them as data/child tables with no controller class
confirmed.claim: 00-DEMO.md line 186 / RESULTS framing: "20 of the 799 doctypes have no controller class (data/child tables); their CRUD is pure Rust."
confirmed.evidence: The 20 unregistered doctypes are exactly the controllers whose base class resolves to Stub (inherit NestedSet/WebsiteGenerator/etc.). Verified all 20 DO define a controller class (unreg_with_class=20, unreg_no_class=0) and all 20 are real masters, not child/data tables (`istable=0, issingle=0` for every one). They include Account, Employee, BOM, Company, Warehouse, Cost Center, Item Group, Customer Group, Supplier Group, Department, Territory, Task, Goal, Job Opening, Quality Procedure, Bank Statement Import, Sales Person, Sales Partner, Location, CRM Sales Hierarchy. AST scan shows substantial dropped lifecycle logic, e.g. BOM drops {before_validate, validate, on_submit, on_cancel, on_update, on_update_after_submit}; Employee drops {validate, before_insert, after_insert, after_rename, on_trash, on_update}; Account drops {validate, on_update, on_trash}. End-to-end proof: POST /api/resource/Account {account_name:Probe, company:NoSuchCo, parent_account:NoSuchParent, is_group:0} returns HTTP 200 and creates the row, although Account.validate (validate_mandatory -> "Root Type is mandatory"; validate_parent -> parent existence) would reject it.
confirmed.fix: Correct the claim: these 20 are master doctypes whose controller logic is dropped because their framework base class is stubbed, not data tables. Either port the framework base classes (NestedSet, WebsiteGenerator) so these register, or explicitly enumerate them as a known no-op gap in the honesty section.
confirmed.reasoning: The finding is fully substantiated by both code reading and live execution. Root cause: ferro_boot._register_module_controllers (ferro_boot.py:128-135) and lazy_import_controller (ferro_boot.py:178-190) only register a controller when issubclass(obj, frappe.model.document.Document) is True. But the 20 affected controllers subclass framework base classes (NestedSet, WebsiteGenerator, DataImport) that the demo's _LazyFinder stubs to frappe._lazy.Stub (a metaclass-based permissive type). A class like `class Account(NestedSet)` therefore becomes a subclass of Stub, NOT of Document, so it silently fails the issubclass gate and never registers — its validate/on_update/on_trash/etc. never run. I reproduced the exact numbers using the real shim+ferro_boot: 779 controllers register, 20 do not (unreg_with_class=20, unreg_no_class=0), and all 20 have istable=0 and issingle=0 (i.e. they are master doctypes, NOT data/child tables). The 20-doctype list matches the finding verbatim (Account, BOM, Bank Statement Import, CRM Sales Hierarchy, Company, Cost Center, Customer Group, Department, Employee, Goal, Item Group, Job Opening, Location, Quality Procedure, Sales Partner, Sales Person, Supplier Group, Task, Territory, Warehouse). The dropped lifecycle sets match too (BOM drops before_validate/on_cancel/on_submit/on_update/on_update_after_submit/validate; Employee drops validate/before_insert/after_insert/after_rename/on_trash/on_update; Account drops validate/on_update/on_trash). The bug holds in BOTH modes: in eager mode the registry never lists these events so the write takes the pure-Rust path; in the recommended lazy mode the AST scan DOES list the events and routes the write to Python, but lazy_import_controller('Account') returns None (class still fails issubclass), so doc.run_method('validate') hits the no-op base Document (document.py:209-213) — still dropping the logic. End-to-end against the prebuilt binary: POST /api/resource/Account {account_name:AuditProbe, company:NoSuchCo, parent_account:NoSuchParent, is_group:0} returned HTTP 200 and created the row (name=444744230b, root_type=null), even though the real Account.validate->validate_mandatory throws "Root Type is mandatory" (account.py:457-459) and validate_parent rejects a nonexistent parent. The report claim at 00-DEMO.md:190-191 ("20 of the 799 doctypes have no controller class (data/child tables); their CRUD is pure Rust") is therefore wrong on two factual counts (they DO have controller classes; they are masters not data/child tables) and its benign framing hides a silent, complete loss of master-controller business logic. It also contradicts the honesty section's own promise (00-DEMO.md:181) that "the app controller's own lifecycle methods execute as real Python." This is a genuine, critical overstatement/error.

confirmed.title: _run_event swallows non-Validation exceptions, so even registered controllers' validate can silently no-op when it touches a stub
confirmed.claim: 00-DEMO.md line 25-28 / line 176-183: "writes drive the real app controllers (validate/before_save/on_update/...)" and "app business logic runs."
confirmed.evidence: shim/ferro_boot.py:300-307 `_run_event` does `try: doc.run_method(event) except (ValidationError, PermissionError): raise; except Exception: pass`. Demonstrated: a controller method raising TypeError is swallowed and the write proceeds. Many registered controllers' validate call into un-ported helpers (e.g. CRM Deal.validate calls self.update_exchange_rate(), apply_sla(), share_with_agent()); if any raises a non-Validation error on a stub, all subsequent validation in that method is skipped and the document still saves. The 141 stubbed modules (boot summary `stubbed: 141`) make this a live path, not theoretical. Only 311 of 779 registered controllers even override a lifecycle method, so the headline "779 controllers run" conflates 'imported' with 'business logic executes to completion'.
confirmed.fix: Do not blanket-swallow controller exceptions; at minimum log/surface them (or fail the write) so a partially-executed validate is not silently treated as a pass. Disclose in the honesty section that controller methods may abort midway on a stub and that abort is swallowed.
confirmed.reasoning:
The finding is substantiated by code and reproduction. /home/frappe/ferro-demo/shim/ferro_boot.py:300-307 (`_run_event`) does exactly: `try: doc.run_method(event); except (frappe.ValidationError, frappe.PermissionError): raise; except Exception: pass`. So any non-Validation/non-Permission exception raised inside a controller lifecycle method is silently swallowed and the write proceeds (ferro_rt.insert/update is called after _run_event in dispatch_write).

I reproduced this with the REAL shim exception classes (/home/frappe/ferro-demo/shim/frappe/exceptions.py) and the exact _run_event logic: IndexError, TypeError, KeyError, AttributeError are all SWALLOWED (write proceeds); only ValidationError/PermissionError and their subclasses (MandatoryError, DoesNotExistError) propagate. This is not theoretical: CRM Deal.validate (crm_deal.py:83-96) calls validate_status() which does `frappe.get_all("CRM Deal Status", {"type":"Open"}, pluck="name")[0]` — a plain IndexError if no Open status exists — before the real enforcement in validate_forecasting_fields/validate_lost_reason/update_exchange_rate runs. A swallow there abandons the rest of validate while the doc still saves. Stub interactions (frappe._lazy.Stub) likewise produce TypeError/AttributeError that get swallowed.

The live binary confirms the quantitative context: boot summary reports controllers: 779, doctypes: 799, import_errors: 0, stubbed: 141 (exactly as the finding cites), and needs-python: 329 doctypes — so well under half the 779 registered controllers carry any lifecycle Python, supporting the 'imported != business-logic-executes-to-completion' point.

This is a genuine overstatement against the report's claims: 00-DEMO.md lines 26-28 ('writes drive the real app controllers (validate/before_save/on_update/...)') and line 188 ('app business logic runs; framework side-effects are deferred'). The honesty section (lines 181-188) frames the only deferred behavior as stub touches that 'no-op' (line 185); it never discloses that a controller's validate can ABORT PARTWAY on a plain exception, that the abort is silently swallowed, and that the write still commits. grep over 00-DEMO.md confirms no mention of swallow/silently/abort/partial/skip. So 'business logic runs' is overstated: it may run partially and then be silently abandoned while the write is treated as a pass.

One imprecision: the finding's '311 of 779' is slightly off (my AST count: 331 controllers override >=1 lifecycle method; binary reports 329 needs-python doctypes). This secondary figure is wrong by ~18-20, but it is directionally correct (well under half) and not load-bearing for the core finding. The suggested fix (don't blanket-swallow; surface/log or fail the write, and disclose the partial-abort behavior) is appropriate.

confirmed.title: Honesty section discloses the wrong stubbing boundary (deep helpers / optional deps) and omits the more severe class-level dropping
confirmed.claim: 00-DEMO.md lines 176-183: stubbing is framed as 'un-ported framework internals (deep frappe.* helpers, heavy optional deps like bs4/twilio) hits the shim's permissive lazy stub and no-ops ... So app business logic runs; framework side-effects are deferred.'
confirmed.evidence: The disclosed boundary is 'a controller calls a deep helper that no-ops.' The actual, undisclosed boundary is that an entire controller's base class can be a stub, causing the whole controller (and all its business logic) to be dropped (20 cases, proven above), and that mid-validate exceptions are swallowed (ferro_boot.py:306-307). These are not 'framework side-effects' like email/PDF — they are core business validations (e.g. Account.validate_mandatory, BOM company check, CRMSalesHierarchy duplicate-user, Employee validation). The phrase 'app business logic runs; framework side-effects are deferred' is therefore misleading for the NestedSet/WebsiteGenerator-derived doctypes and for any controller whose validate aborts on a stub.
confirmed.fix: Rewrite the honesty section to state explicitly: (1) controllers whose base class is an un-ported framework class (NestedSet, WebsiteGenerator, etc.) are not registered and run zero Python — list them; (2) controller methods that raise on a stub are silently swallowed, so business logic may partially or fully not execute even for registered controllers.
confirmed.reasoning:
The finding is substantiated and, if anything, understated. The honesty section of 00-DEMO.md frames the stubbing boundary as "a controller calls a deep frappe.* helper / heavy optional dep (bs4/twilio) which no-ops" and concludes (line 188) "app business logic runs; framework side-effects are deferred." It then disposes of the 20-doctype gap with the false claim (line 191) that "20 of the 799 doctypes have no controller class (data/child tables); their CRUD is pure Rust."

Runtime verification refutes that disclosure on every point:

(1) Whole-controller dropping is real, 20 cases. Running the binary: `controllers: 779, doctypes: 799`. Replaying the exact discovery+registration logic shows all 20 "missing" doctypes DO have a controller class in their .py file — none are child/data tables. `istable=False` for all 20; they are large top-level business DocTypes, mostly tree doctypes (Company 132 fields, Employee 109, BOM 94, Task 51). They are dropped because `_register_module_controllers` (ferro_boot.py:128-135) requires `issubclass(obj, frappe.model.document.Document)`, and their base class resolves to the permissive Stub: 16 have `stub_in_mro=True` (NestedSet/WebsiteGenerator/DataImport-derived: Company, Cost Center, Customer Group, Department, Item Group, Location, Quality Procedure, Sales Partner, Sales Person, Supplier Group, Territory, Warehouse, CRM Sales Hierarchy, Goal, Job Opening, Bank Statement Import), and 4 (Account, BOM, Employee, Task) drop because the loop instead picks an exception class (RootNotEditable, BOMRecursionError, EmployeeUserDisabledError, CircularReferenceError) that also isn't a Document subclass. So Account.validate->validate_mandatory, BOM recursion checks, CRMSalesHierarchy.validate, Employee validation, etc. run ZERO Python — these are core business validations, not email/PDF side-effects, so "app business logic runs" is false for them.

(2) The report contradicts itself: line 183 cites `CRMSalesHierarchy.validate` as one of three "proven" cases of the controller's own lifecycle running as real Python — but CRMSalesHierarchy subclasses NestedSet, resolves to Stub, and is one of the 20 silently-dropped controllers (verified registered=False at runtime). verify.sh/VERIFY.txt only exercises favorable controllers that subclass Document directly (RetentionBonus, CRM Deal) and never touches a NestedSet/WebsiteGenerator doctype, so the drop is never surfaced.

(3) Mid-validate swallowing is real (ferro_boot.py:304-320): `_run_event` re-raises only frappe.ValidationError/PermissionError and `pass`es every other exception, so a registered controller's validate that raises on a stub (e.g. AttributeError, or a dynamically-synthesized FrappeException subclass that is NOT a ValidationError per exceptions.py __getattr__) aborts silently while the Rust write still persists.

The line-191 "data/child tables" claim is demonstrably wrong, and the qualitative framing minimizes a severe, undisclosed correctness boundary. High severity is justified.

confirmed.title: Python dispatch path silently drops all child-table rows on insert/update (data loss)
confirmed.claim: 00-DEMO.md: 'writes drive the real app controllers ... in embedded CPython' and 'Reads and pure-CRUD writes are fully real' — i.e. a needs-Python write persists the document correctly.
confirmed.evidence: shim/frappe/model/document.py:125-137 get_valid_dict() excludes child tables (`if key in tables ... continue` and `if isinstance(val, list): continue`). ferro_boot.py:335 and :360 persist via `ferro_rt.insert/update(doctype, json.dumps(doc.get_valid_dict()))`, so children never reach orm::insert_children. Verified live: POST /api/resource/Contact with email_ids+phone_nos via the Python path (--apps crm --load all, Contact.validate is Python) returned `email_ids: []`, `phone_nos: []`; the identical payload on the pure-Rust path (--apps '' --load none) returned both child arrays populated. Because erpnext registers wildcard 'validate' (boot log: `needs-python: ... wildcard={validate, on_trash}`), EVERY write in the all-5-apps config routes through this lossy Python path, so any doctype with child tables (Sales Invoice items, Sales Order, etc.) loses its child rows.
confirmed.fix: In dispatch_write, send the full document (doc.as_dict(), which includes child arrays) to ferro_rt.insert/update instead of get_valid_dict(); or have get_valid_dict keep child tables for the persistence call. Ensure orm::insert_children/child-replace runs on the Python path identically to the Rust path.
confirmed.reasoning: The finding is fully substantiated structurally and by live reproduction. (1) shim/frappe/model/document.py:125-137 get_valid_dict() excludes child tables: line 132 `if key in tables or isinstance(val, BaseDocument): continue` and line 134-135 `if isinstance(val, list): continue`. (2) ferro_boot.py:335 (insert) and :360 (update) persist via `ferro_rt.insert/update(..., json.dumps(doc.get_valid_dict()))`, so child arrays never reach the ORM. (3) On the Rust side, orm.rs:690 insert_children does `data.get(&cf.fieldname).and_then(|v| v.as_array())` and `continue`s when the key is absent — so stripped children are silently not written; orm::update similarly only replaces child arrays present in the payload. (4) Routing in ferrod.rs:336/356: a write goes to run_py_write (the lossy path) whenever `registry.needs(doctype, INSERT/UPDATE_EVENTS)`; the pure-Rust orm::insert at :343 is given the FULL data (children intact). erpnext registers wildcard `validate`, so in the all-5-apps config every write with a validate event routes through the lossy Python path. Live boot log confirmed `wildcard={on_trash, validate}`. This contradicts 00-DEMO.md's 'pure-CRUD writes are fully real' / 'writes drive the real app controllers' claims. It is a genuine critical data-loss bug.

confirmed.title: Non-child doctypes whose physical table lacks parent/parentfield/parenttype columns return three bogus fields on every read and write
confirmed.claim: build_db.py docstring: 'a faithful ... re-implementation' and meta.rs STANDARD_COLUMNS; the implicit claim that reads return the document's real fields.
confirmed.evidence: meta.rs:12-15 + 156 unconditionally put `parent`,`parentfield`,`parenttype` into Meta.columns. orm.rs get_doc (line 411/418) and get_list build the SELECT from meta.columns. For a non-child doctype whose table omits those columns, SQLite's double-quoted-identifier-falls-back-to-string-literal misfeature makes `SELECT "parent"` return the literal string 'parent' with the column header `"parent"`. Verified: `SELECT name,"parent" FROM tabContact` -> ('3796c6b40b','parent'); GET/POST Contact (both Rust and Python paths) return `"\"parent\"": "parent"`, `"\"parentfield\"": "parentfield"`, `"\"parenttype\"": "parenttype"`. 146 of 989 tab* tables in the demo DB lack a parent column (the pre-existing frappe-core doctypes: Contact, ToDo, User, ...), so this bug fires on ~15% of doctypes including ones the demo exercises (ToDo). VERIFY.txt test #5 ('ToDo read works in Rust') passes only because it checks request success, not field correctness.
confirmed.fix: Restrict the SELECT/columns set to columns actually present in the table (use the PRAGMA table_info result as the authoritative column set for non-single/non-virtual doctypes instead of unioning STANDARD_COLUMNS), or guard each standard column with meta.has_physical_column() before selecting. Long term, disable SQLite's double-quote-as-string fallback or build SELECT lists only from PRAGMA-confirmed columns.

The finding is fully substantiated by code reading and live binary execution; I could not refute any sub-claim.

Mechanism (code): meta.rs:12-15 defines STANDARD_COLUMNS including "parent","parentfield","parenttype". load_meta (meta.rs:156) seeds `columns` from ALL of STANDARD_COLUMNS unconditionally, then the PRAGMA table_info loop (meta.rs:162-170) only INSERTS physical columns — it never intersects/removes — so for a non-child table whose physical schema omits those three, they remain in `meta.columns`. get_doc (orm.rs:410-418) builds the SELECT list directly from `meta.columns` filtered only by ACL, quoting each with quote_ident (meta.rs:73-84) which emits double quotes. `SELECT "parent"` against a table with no such column triggers SQLite's double-quote-identifier→string-literal fallback, yielding the literal value 'parent' under the header '"parent"'. The same column set drives get_list.

Empirical (DB): tabContact, tabToDo, tabUser have ZERO of the three parent columns; `SELECT name,"parent","parentfield","parenttype" FROM tabContact` returns ('3796c6b40b','parent','parentfield','parenttype') with headers ['name','"parent"','"parentfield"','"parenttype"']. 146 of 989 tab* tables lack a parent column (~15%), matching the finding's count exactly.

Empirical (live ferrod binary): GET /api/resource/Contact/<name>, GET /api/resource/ToDo/<name>, the list endpoint (default and fields=["*"] and fields=["name","parent"]), AND POST create-ToDo all return `"\"parent\"": "parent"`, `"\"parentfield\"": "parentfield"`, `"\"parenttype\"": "parenttype"` — confirming the bug fires on every read AND write path, in the pure-Rust read path and the controller write path alike.

Faithfulness divergence is genuine: real Frappe gives every doctype table these columns (typically null), so the demo's '"parent": "parent"' literals are wrong both vs Frappe and as data. VERIFY.txt test #5 ("ToDo read works in Rust") only greps for '"data"', so it passes despite the corrupt fields, exactly as the finding states. Severity high is reasonable: corrupted/extra fields on ~15% of doctypes including demo-exercised ones, silently.

confirmed.title: override_doctype_class is parsed but never instantiated or counted in the needs-Python registry
confirmed.claim: 00-DEMO.md architecture table: ferro_boot 'parses each app's hooks.py and merges doc_events / overrides'; the claim that the apps' real controllers run.
confirmed.evidence: ferro_boot.py:159-161 stores override_doctype_class into _OVERRIDE_CLASS, but shim/frappe/__init__.py _new_controller (lines 310-318) only consults _CONTROLLER_REGISTRY / _lazy_import_controller — never _OVERRIDE_CLASS. needs_python_registry() (ferro_boot.py:247-276) likewise never inspects _OVERRIDE_CLASS. Confirmed real overrides exist: crm {Contact->CustomContact, Email Template->...}, helpdesk {Email Account->CustomEmailAccount}, hrms {Employee->EmployeeMaster, Timesheet->EmployeeTimesheet, Payment Entry->EmployeePaymentEntry, Project->EmployeeProject}. So frappe.get_doc('Employee', ...) instantiates the base Employee controller, not hrms' EmployeeMaster. It is non-corrupting for these five apps ONLY because the inspected override classes add no lifecycle methods (AST shows lifecycle=[]); but the registry would take the Rust fast path for any override that DOES add validate/on_update on a base doctype that otherwise has none.
confirmed.fix: Register override_doctype_class targets into _CONTROLLER_REGISTRY (resolving the dotted class) so _new_controller uses them, and include their MRO-visible lifecycle methods when building needs_python_registry().
confirmed.reasoning: The finding is a genuine, accurately-scoped overstatement of fidelity in 00-DEMO.md's claim that ferro_boot 'merges ... overrides' and that the apps' real controllers run. Verified by reading the code: override_doctype_class is parsed and stored into _OVERRIDE_CLASS (ferro_boot.py:159-161) and handed to frappe.boot.set_hooks (line 207), but it is never consulted by the controller-resolution path. _new_controller (frappe/__init__.py:310-318) and get_controller (model/document.py:300-302) only read _CONTROLLER_REGISTRY (+ _lazy_import_controller), and needs_python_registry (ferro_boot.py:247-276) only inspects _CONTROLLER_REGISTRY / _AST_EVENTS / _MERGED_DOC_EVENTS. There is no grep hit for _OVERRIDE_CLASS in either consumer. Because override files live under app/overrides/ (not app/.../doctype/<name>/<name>.py), discover_doctypes' glob never finds them, so frappe.get_doc('Employee', ...) instantiates the base Employee controller (registered from erpnext via discovery), never hrms' EmployeeMaster. The finding's correctness caveat also checks out: every override class has lifecycle=[] (they add only non-lifecycle methods such as autoname/set_status/default_list_data/get_inbound_mails), so for these five apps the needs-Python registry is not made unsound by the omission. I tried to refute via the implicit objection that the override classes subclass bases with lifecycle methods (so the doctype is in needs-Python anyway via the base) — that is true and means this is a behavioral-fidelity gap (override-added method bodies like EmployeeMaster.autoname are silently skipped), not a Rust-fast-path corruption for these apps. That nuance is exactly what the finding already states. The suggested fix (register override targets into _CONTROLLER_REGISTRY and include their MRO-visible lifecycle in needs_python_registry) is correct. Severity medium is appropriate.

confirmed.title: Eager and lazy modes compute different needs-Python registries; lazy AST-scan misses inherited lifecycle methods
confirmed.claim: 00-DEMO.md: 'AST-scanning the controllers ... build the needs-Python registry ... exact without paying the import cost'; lazy is the 'recommended' deployment.
confirmed.evidence: Eager path (ferro_boot.py:255-263) uses getattr(cls, ev) is not base — MRO-aware, sees inherited methods. Lazy path uses _ast_scan_events (lines 109-122) which only collects methods defined DIRECTLY in a ClassDef in the leaf file, so a controller that inherits validate from a base (e.g. erpnext SellingController/AccountsController) without redefining it is NOT flagged. Measured divergence: all-apps eager=329 doctypes vs lazy=346; crm-only eager=28 vs lazy=29 (boot logs). The AST scan also over-includes test classes (it does not filter by issubclass(Document) the way _register_module_controllers does). In the all-5-apps config the inheritance gap is masked by erpnext's wildcard 'validate', but a non-erpnext lazy deployment could take the Rust fast path and skip an inherited validate — a registry false-negative.
confirmed.fix: Make the AST scan resolve base classes (or fall back to importing controllers whose bases are non-trivial) so inherited lifecycle methods are detected; alternatively have lazy mode reuse the eager MRO-based introspection on first touch and treat any unresolved inheritance conservatively (route to Python). Filter scanned classes to Document subclasses to avoid spurious test-class inclusions.
confirmed.reasoning: The finding's core technical claims all check out, and I found a concrete unmasked behavioral divergence that even strengthens it. (1) Eager uses MRO-aware introspection (ferro_boot.py:255-263, getattr(cls,ev) is not base); lazy uses _ast_scan_events (109-122) which walks ast.ClassDef and only collects methods defined DIRECTLY in the leaf file -- confirmed in code. (2) Lazy therefore misses inherited lifecycle methods: traced 39 erpnext doctypes (e.g. Asset.on_change from TransactionBase; Delivery Note/Serial No on_update from StockController, before_cancel/on_cancel from AccountsController) that eager sees and lazy does not. (3) The measured divergence is exactly as cited -- I reproduced via the prebuilt binary: all-apps eager=329 vs lazy=346 (wildcard {validate,on_trash}), crm-only eager=28 vs lazy=29. (4) The AST scan has no issubclass(Document) filter (it walks every ClassDef) -- 18 over-included doctypes measured. (5) The shim comment 'the needs-Python registry is exact without paying the import cost' (ferro_boot.py:231) is an overstatement: the lazy registry diverges from the eager ground truth in 39 false-negative-event doctypes + 18 over-included ones. Critically, I confirmed a REAL, unmasked dispatch divergence in a shipped config: in hrms-only lazy mode (no erpnext hooks => empty wildcard), Gratuity and Leave Encashment inherit a REAL AccountsController.on_trash; their lazy registry is {validate,on_cancel,on_submit} with no on_trash, so a DELETE routes to Rust and SKIPS the inherited Python on_trash, whereas eager routes to Python -- exactly the false-negative the finding warned about. Minor inaccuracies that don't undermine it: the literal 'exact' phrase is in ferro_boot.py:231 not 00-DEMO.md (still the audited demo; 00-DEMO.md line 150-152 promotes AST-scan lazy as the operative/recommended lever); the cited crm 28-vs-29 example is actually lazy over-inclusion (a NestedSet doctype eager drops) rather than the inheritance gap, and the concrete over-includes are NestedSet doctypes not 'test classes' (though the missing-Document-filter mechanism is genuine). The all-5-apps insert/update path is masked by the validate wildcard, but the delete path in hrms-only is genuinely unmasked. Medium severity is fair: a reproducible correctness defect that silently skips inherited erpnext lifecycle logic in a legitimate single-app lazy deployment, contradicting the 'exact' claim.

confirmed.title: Submit/cancel/rename lifecycle hooks can never fire — no route invokes those ops
confirmed.claim: 00-DEMO.md architecture: ferro 'drives the controller lifecycle for a hooked write, calling Python at the populated trigger points'.
confirmed.evidence: dispatch_write (ferro_boot.py:342-381) handles op in {update,submit,cancel,delete}, but route_resource (ferrod.rs:318-388) only ever calls run_py_write with op 'insert'/'update'/'delete' — there is no POST .../submit or rename endpoint, and registry.needs is only checked against INSERT_EVENTS/UPDATE_EVENTS/DELETE_EVENTS (ferrod.rs:93-97), which exclude on_submit/on_cancel/on_update_after_submit/before_rename/after_rename. Real hooks registered on those events exist: hrms Payment Entry {on_submit,on_cancel,on_update_after_submit}, hrms Journal Entry {on_submit,on_update_after_submit,on_cancel}, crm Item / helpdesk Customer {before_rename,after_rename}. These never execute. This aligns with ferro's documented REST limitations but is not called out in the lifecycle claim.
confirmed.fix: Either expose submit/cancel/rename endpoints that drive the corresponding ops, or explicitly document in 00-DEMO.md that submit/cancel/rename lifecycle events are out of scope (currently only the validate-before-naming divergence is disclosed).
confirmed.reasoning:
The finding is accurate and well-substantiated. There is a genuine asymmetry: the Python side (ferro_boot.py) is fully wired to drive submit/cancel/rename lifecycle events and registers them in the needs-Python registry, but the Rust router can never reach them.

Verified directly:
- dispatch_write (ferro_boot.py:342-381) implements op in {update,submit,cancel,delete} including before_submit/on_submit/before_cancel/on_cancel. The submit/cancel branches are dead code from the router's perspective.
- route_resource (ferrod.rs:318-388) maps only GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE to insert/update/delete; run_py_write is only ever called with "insert"/"update"/"delete". There is no submit/cancel/rename endpoint.
- /api/method/ (ferrod.rs:266-274) is allow-listed to ping + get_logged_user; any other method => 404. No *.submit or rename method.
- INSERT_EVENTS/UPDATE_EVENTS/DELETE_EVENTS (ferrod.rs:93-97) exclude on_submit, on_cancel, on_update_after_submit, before_rename, after_rename. So registry.needs is never consulted for those events.
- The Python registry (needs_python_registry ferro_boot.py:247-276 + LIFECYCLE_EVENTS 168-172) DOES include all those events, so they are genuinely populated trigger points — the demo's claim ('calling Python at the populated trigger points', 00-DEMO.md:104) is overstated relative to what any route can actually trigger.
- grep across all top-level ferro/src/*.rs finds NO submit/cancel/rename route (only a permission ptype string match in auth.rs and a comment in orm.rs).

Real hooks confirmed to exist (so this is not vacuous): erpnext Payment Entry on_submit/on_update_after_submit/on_cancel + hrms doc_events (hrms/hooks.py:182-188); erpnext Journal Entry before_submit/on_submit/on_update_after_submit/on_cancel + hrms hooks (190-198); crm Item before_rename/after_rename (crm/hooks.py:187-191); helpdesk Customer/HD Customer before_rename/after_rename (helpdesk/hooks.py:76-77, hd_customer.py:78-81). Minor attribution nit: Payment Entry/Journal Entry controllers live in erpnext, not hrms — but hrms genuinely registers those submit/cancel hooks via doc_events on those doctypes, so the finding's framing is substantively correct.

Disclosure gap confirmed: 00-DEMO.md/RESULTS.txt/VERIFY.txt contain zero mentions of submit/cancel/rename/docstatus. The only disclosed write-lifecycle divergence is validate-before-naming (00-DEMO.md:192-194). The LIMITATIONS.md catch-all reference (00-DEMO.md:195-196) enumerates 'child-row name preservation, optimistic concurrency, link-integrity on delete' — not submit/cancel/rename.

Refutation attempt: The strongest counter is ferro/LIMITATIONS.md:9-12 ('No controller business logic... submit-cancel returns 405'). But that line describes the pure-Rust REST runtime where NO controller logic runs at all — whereas the demo explicitly DOES run insert/update/on_trash hooks. So that line is not a faithful description of the demo's hybrid behavior, and the demo's own lifecycle claim does not carve out submit/cancel/rename. The refutation fails. Severity 'low' is appropriate: it's a scope/disclosure-completeness gap, not a crash or data-corruption bug.

confirmed.title: DEMO mis-attributes the '*'.on_trash wildcard hook to erpnext; it actually comes from gameplan
confirmed.claim: 00-DEMO.md line 107: "(erpnext registers '*'.validate and '*'.on_trash, so with erpnext loaded every write consults Python — the SLA/deletion-lock hooks — exactly as real Frappe does; reads stay in Rust.)"

The '*'.on_trash wildcard is `gameplan.mixins.on_delete.on_trash`, registered by gameplan, not erpnext. The runtime confirms the merged wildcard is {validate, on_trash} but the on_trash half is gameplan's, not erpnext's. The doc's parenthetical 'the SLA/deletion-lock hooks' is also muddled: both the SLA (service_level_agreement.apply) AND the deletion-lock (transaction_deletion_record check) are erpnext '*'.validate hooks; neither is an on_trash hook.
confirmed.fix: Correct line 107 to: erpnext registers '*'.validate (SLA apply + deletion-lock check), and gameplan registers '*'.on_trash (soft-delete mixin) — so with both apps loaded every write/delete consults Python. Remove the false claim that erpnext registers '*'.on_trash.
confirmed.reasoning:
The finding is substantiated by the source. 00-DEMO.md (lines 105-107) states: "(erpnext registers `'*'.validate` and `'*'.on_trash`, so with erpnext loaded every write consults Python — the SLA/deletion-lock hooks ...)". This is factually wrong on the on_trash half:

1. erpnext's hooks.py doc_events '*' block (lines 352-357) contains ONLY a `validate` key with two functions: service_level_agreement.apply and transaction_deletion_record.check_for_running_deletion_job. It registers NO '*'.on_trash. erpnext does have on_trash hooks, but only scoped to specific doctypes (Sales Invoice line 393, Payment Entry line 402, Contact line 410), never the '*' wildcard.
2. The '*'.on_trash wildcard actually comes from gameplan (gameplan/hooks.py lines 142-145): `'on_trash': 'gameplan.mixins.on_delete.on_trash'`. So the merged runtime wildcard {validate, on_trash} pairs erpnext's validate with gameplan's on_trash; the doc attributes both to erpnext.
3. The parenthetical "the SLA/deletion-lock hooks" is also muddled: both named hooks (SLA apply + deletion-lock check) are erpnext '*'.validate hooks; neither is an on_trash hook. The deletion-lock function's own docstring says "Hook function called on document validate". So the doc mismatches the event list (validate + on_trash) against two hooks that are both validate.

I tried to refute it by searching for any other doc_events/'*' assignment in erpnext and any on_trash under erpnext's wildcard; none exists. The finding holds. The suggested fix is accurate. Note the cited line is 107 but the full sentence spans 105-107 — minor, the substance is correct.

confirmed.title: Lazy-mode needs-Python registry is described as 'exact' but over-counts by 17 doctypes vs eager
confirmed.claim: 00-DEMO.md lines 150-152: lazy AST-scan "Build the needs-Python registry by AST-scanning the controllers (no import)" ... "so the needs-Python registry is exact without paying the import cost" (ferro_boot.py line 232 comment also says 'exact').
confirmed.evidence: Runtime output: eager mode reports `needs-python: 329 doctypes`; lazy mode reports `needs-python: 346 doctypes` for the identical app set. The AST scan (ferro_boot.py `_ast_scan_events`, line 109-122) flags any class method whose name is a lifecycle event, whereas eager introspection (needs_python_registry, line 257-262) only counts a method when `m is not base` (the bound method differs from Document's base). Lazy therefore over-counts by 17. It is safe/conservative (never under-counts, so no write incorrectly skips Python) but it is not 'exact'.
confirmed.fix: Replace 'exact' with 'conservative (a safe over-approximation): AST name-matching may flag a few methods that introspection would dedup against the base class, so lazy routes >= the set eager would (346 vs 329) — never fewer.'
confirmed.reasoning:
The core claim is TRUE and substantiated by runtime: for the identical app set, eager reports `needs-python: 329 doctypes` and lazy reports `needs-python: 346 doctypes` (gap = exactly 17). The word "exact" describing the needs-Python registry genuinely appears at /home/frappe/ferro-demo/shim/ferro_boot.py:231 ("so the needs-Python registry is exact without paying the import cost"). Since lazy and eager disagree by 17 for the same input, "exact" is an overstatement; lazy is in fact a conservative over-approximation. Lazy is safe: it never under-counts (AST flags a superset), so no hooked write incorrectly skips Python. The suggested fix (replace "exact" with "conservative over-approximation, 346 >= 329, never fewer") is substantively correct. So the finding is a genuine, if low-severity, doc/code-comment overstatement.

TWO caveats that weaken the finding's evidence but not its core verdict:
(1) Misattributed quote: the finding says the "exact" phrase is at "00-DEMO.md lines 150-152". I verified those lines (they describe "AST-scanning the controllers (no import)") but they do NOT contain the word "exact". The "exact" claim lives only in the code comment ferro_boot.py:231, which the finding does also cite. So the DEMO.md citation is wrong; the code citation is right.
(2) Wrong mechanism: the finding attributes the 17-doctype over-count to the eager `m is not base` dedup (line 260). This is incorrect. AST scan only flags a class that PHYSICALLY defines a lifecycle method in its body (ferro_boot.py:120); for any physically-defined method `getattr(cls,ev) is not getattr(Document,ev)` is always True, so `m is not base` can never dedup an AST-flagged method. The real cause is that eager registers only 779/799 controllers: controllers whose base class is an intermediate like NestedSet/AccountsController/TransactionBase (I found 66 controllers-with-lifecycle-methods whose direct base is not `Document`) fail `issubclass(obj,_Document)` when that base module is stubbed (eager stubbed=141 modules), so they never enter `_CONTROLLER_REGISTRY` and eager's introspection loop (lines 255-263) never sees them — while lazy's base-agnostic AST scan counts them anyway.

Net: the overstatement is real and the fix is correct, but the finding's explanatory evidence (the `m is not base` mechanism and the 00-DEMO.md line citation) is partly inaccurate.
